relationships.description: The retention policy groups the collection into its scope set, so one lifecycle rule covers several independently existing collections without owning them.
relationships.evidence: The policy definition lists the collection by name in its scope, for example several hypertables passed to TimescaleDB add_retention_policy, or an Elasticsearch ILM policy attached to the index through an index template.

relationships.description: The retention policy includes the whole namespace in its scope, so every collection created under that schema, keyspace or database falls within the rule.
relationships.evidence: The policy is declared at namespace level, for example an InfluxDB CREATE RETENTION POLICY ... ON <database> or a bucket retention period, and lists the namespace as its target.

relationships.description: When records pass the policy's maximum age, the archive action moves them out of the live data into this designated archive collection.
relationships.evidence: The policy's action is set to archive and names the target table or index, for example a pg_partman retention_schema setting or a scheduled INSERT INTO archive_table ... DELETE job tied to the policy.

relationships.description: The retention policy dictates how long records may remain in the collection and what happens to records older than that age.
relationships.evidence: The collection carries the lifecycle setting, such as a MongoDB TTL index with expireAfterSeconds, a Cassandra table default_time_to_live, or a TimescaleDB retention policy on the hypertable.

relationships.description: The retention policy sets the default record lifetime and expiry action that apply across the collections inside the namespace.
relationships.evidence: The namespace's configuration names the policy as its default lifecycle rule, for example the default retention policy of an InfluxDB database or an ILM policy bound to an index pattern covering the namespace.

relationships.description: The policy's maximum age and disposal action keep stored data within a mandated limit, such as a jurisdictional data-minimisation rule or a storage budget ceiling.
relationships.evidence: A decision record or constraint register entry is cited by the policy, and the configured retention duration and action match the limit that the constraint states.

relationships.description: The policy honours the data-retention or deletion terms agreed in the contract, such as a data processing agreement that requires customer data to be purged within a set period.
relationships.evidence: The contract clause is referenced in the policy documentation, and the configured maximum age is equal to or shorter than the period the contract specifies.

relationships.description: The policy puts into practice an enterprise principle such as 'retain data no longer than necessary' for the collections it covers.
relationships.evidence: The architecture principles catalogue or an ADR links the principle to this policy, giving the policy as its concrete application in the data store.

relationships.description: The policy realises a verifiable retention requirement, for example 'session records shall be deleted after 30 days'.
relationships.evidence: The requirement ID appears in the policy's migration or configuration comments, and an automated test or audit query shows that no records older than the required age remain.

relationships.description: The data-store policy carries out the security retention rule by keeping the security-relevant data at least as long as the rule's minimum and disposing of it by the method the rule prescribes.
relationships.evidence: The audit-log or evidence collection's configured TTL or retention period is greater than or equal to the minimum in the security policy, and a mapping in the compliance documentation links the two policies.

relationships.description: Enforcing the policy (expiring, deleting or moving records) produces data-change events that cause the event handler bound to the governed collection to fire.
relationships.evidence: A DELETE trigger or change-stream/CDC subscription on the governed collection filters for, or is documented as reacting to, the removals that the retention job or TTL monitor performs.

relationships.description: The policy's scheduled enforcement invokes the stored logic that carries out its action, such as an archive, downsample or purge procedure.
relationships.evidence: A scheduler entry tied to the policy calls the procedure by name, for example TimescaleDB add_job, a pg_cron schedule, or a continuous-aggregate refresh that the policy definition references.

relationships.description: The policy relies on an infrastructure capability, such as object-storage lifecycle tiering, a managed-database scheduler or a TTL engine, to apply its expiry action.
relationships.evidence: Infrastructure-as-code or platform configuration enables the service for the policy, for example an S3 lifecycle rule or a managed storage tier declared as the archive or move-tier target.

notes: Aggregates and governs toward Collection and Namespace are redundant. A policy does not contain containers as parts; it scopes and rules them, so governs is the correct predicate and aggregates should be dropped. Satisfies toward security.retentionpolicy holds only when the maximum age is not shorter than the security policy's minimum retention period.
